title: Evaluating Acid Penetration Effects on Geopolymer Integrity Using Microscopy and Microanalysis
content: Concrete is the second-most-used substance in the world, with water being the first. There is a high global demand for concrete and the cement used in concrete called Portland Cement (PC) [1]. PC has an annual global production of approximately 4.6 billion tonnes with predicted growth to 6 billion tonnes by 2050 [1]. However, the production of PC has significant environmental impacts accounting for approx. 8% of global CO2 emissions [2-3] and is vulnerable to acid attack from various sources such as ground water, chemical wastes, sewage systems and acid rain. Acid attack degrades the cement in concrete, which has high amounts of calcium-based phases and jeopardise the structural performance of concrete by eventually causing a premature failure during its expected lifetime [4-5]. For this reason, there is a considerable push to develop greener means of producing PC, as well as alternative cements, and materials called geopolymers that can handle acid attack.
